item.title: [Articles | InfoStealers] FortiBleed 2.0: 975 New Domains & 40,573 Exposed Secrets – Claim Your Ethical Disclosure
item.description: FortiBleed 2.0: 975 New Domains & 40,573 Exposed Secrets – Claim Your Ethical Disclosure | Hudson Rock Hudson Rock Threat Intelligence FortiBleed 2.0 Configuration & Credential Exposure FortiBleed 2.0: 975 New Domains & 40,573 Exposed Secrets – Claim Your Ethical Disclosure Newly obtained FortiGate configuration reports reveal 40,573 records containing cleartext secrets , including 37,076 local-user records and 1,576 Active Directory LDAP bind records . The analysis also identifies 975 domain labels absent from FortiBleed 1.0 . The configuration material dates to around February 2026, earlier than the likely May/June material examined in the first investigation. Earlier Evidence, Obtained Later FortiBleed 2.0 names the follow-up investigation. Researchers obtained the files only recently. In the CSV, 1,672 of the 1,703 source files have report timestamps on February 20, 2026 ; 31 are undated. These are report dates, not independently established dates of first compromise or configuration extraction. The comparison below measures exposure recorded in the datasets, not organizations’ responses to the later FortiBleed 1.0 disclosure. Check your organization: Search the FortiBleed exposure records through Hudson Rock’s free portal. Check Your Domain → Inside the Investigation 01 What the Files Reveal 02 From Configuration Theft to Internal Access 03 How the Datasets Compare 04 What the Overlapping Hosts Reveal 05 Behind the Registration Email 06 The Network Details in the Backup 07 What Affected Organizations Should Check 1. What the Configuration Files Reveal A firewall backup can expose remote-access accounts, the secrets connecting an appliance to Active Directory, and the addresses of internal systems. Across 1,703 configuration-report files , FortiBleed 2.0 shows how much information can become available through administrative access to a network’s perimeter. The combined export contains 101,419 credential and account records associated with 1,689 nonempty host identifiers . Of those records, 40,573 contain cleartext secrets . Local users account for most of that exposure, but the dataset also includes directory bind accounts, administrator logins, SMTP credentials, and HA cluster secrets. Each category connects the firewall to another part of the organization’s infrastructure. 101,419 Credential & Account Records From 1,703 source files associated with 1,689 host identifiers. 40,573 Cleartext Secret Records Across local users, administrator logins, LDAP, SMTP, and HA settings. 1,576 Cleartext LDAP Bind Records Service-account secrets recovered within 2,163 LDAP records. 54.7% Hosts Absent from 1.0 924 of 1,689 host identifiers add coverage beyond the compared perimeter list. Hudson Rock’s first FortiBleed investigation described a much broader perimeter credential list. Rechecking the FortiBleed 1.0 text dataset yields 73,932 login rows across 69,055 host identifiers . The smaller configuration corpus adds depth: the account tables and directory connections behind those logins, plus records for hosts absent from that larger list. Research Credit: NyxLab Hudson Rock credits NyxLab for its foundational technical research into the threat actor known as k0t and the associated extraction tooling. For background on the actor’s operational infrastructure, read NyxLab’s investigation, “Stray Cat, Open Doors: How k0t Wanders Through the Network Edge” Campaign context and the vulnerability timeline FortiCloud SSO abuse is part of the wider campaign context. CVE-2026-24858 (CVSS 9.4) affects FortiOS, FortiProxy, and FortiSwitchManager. Fortinet records issuing its advisory on January 27, 2026 , before the February report timestamps. Its June assessment also discusses reused credentials and brute-force activity. These records do not establish one initial-access mechanism for every host. Related Group-IB and NyxLab research describes victim overlap with Qilin and The Gentlemen. A direct affiliation or supplier relationship remains unconfirmed. 2. From Configuration Theft to Internal Access The associated tooling connects three stages: extracting a configuration, recovering secrets, and attempting access to internal systems. The reports expose the accounts and settings that make this progression possible. Extract the configuration and recover secrets. The parsing workflow described around forti_parse.py collects administrator entries, local users, LDAP connections, HA settings, and email-server credentials. The CSV records 37,076 cleartext local-user entries and 1,576 cleartext LDAP bind entries . It also retains hashes and undecrypted values, so the export distinguishes recovered secrets from values whose cleartext is not present in the export. Attempt VPN access. The reported vpn_checker.py / openconnect workflow uses eligible VPN credentials to attempt connections. The account’s status, VPN policy, MFA requirements, and reachability determine whether a session is possible. Firewall-management privileges and VPN-user permissions are separate. Identify directory servers and assess access. The LDAP server and distinguished-name fields identify directory infrastructure and its bind identities. Research into the associated toolchain describes nxc / NetExec activity against internal systems. An overprivileged bind identity can expose a much wider environment; ordinary LDAP query rights alone do not confer domain-administrator privileges, directory replication rights, or access to NTDS.dit . Why a Backup Can Expose Working Secrets The reports distinguish administrator hashes such as SHA-256 ( SH2 ) and PBKDF2 ( PB2 ) from reversibly encrypted ENC secrets. Configurations using FortiOS’s system-default key can permit offline recovery of stored secrets. Fortinet also supports device-specific private-data-encryption keys , so recoverability depends on the version, settings, and material obtained. Exposure and usable access are different measurements. For example, 7,437 of the 37,076 cleartext local-user records are marked disabled in the CSV. The recovered secret remains part of the exposure, while that status changes how the corresponding login should be assessed. Figure 1: A redacted parsed report for Hilton-FW / FortiGate-60F , registered to @theelysiumhotels.com with the internal domain HILTON.LOCAL . The CSV contains 12 System Admin entries and 10 cleartext local-user records for this source file. The administrator list includes districtadmin , fgtsec , fortiadmin , forticloud-sync , forticloud-tech , fortinet-gbrcc , fortinet-support , and fortinet-tech . The Technical_support login is marked verified in the source report. 3. How the Two Datasets Compare The smaller configuration corpus adds substantial coverage to the perimeter list: 924 of its 1,689 host identifiers (54.7%) are absent from FortiBleed 1.0. Across the three attribution fields used in this analysis, the CSV contains 1,453 distinct domain labels , of which 975 (67.1%) are absent from the 1.0 comparison set. It also adds local-user credentials, directory bind secrets, and configuration details that the perimeter list did not capture. What Is Being Compared FortiBleed 1.0 Perimeter Credential List FortiBleed 2.0 Configuration Records What the Comparison Adds Credential & Account Records 73,932 source login rows 101,419 credential and account records Broader information about the accounts and secrets stored on the appliances Distinct Host Identifiers 69,055 , comprising IP addresses and DNS hostnames 1,689 nonempty host identifiers across 1,703 source reports 924 (54.7%) absent from 1.0; 765 (45.3%) in both datasets Domain Labels Used for Attribution 22,003 labels from FortiGuard registration, DNS fields, and SNMP-contact email domains 1,453 distinct labels from primary attribution, registration emails, and email-format usernames 975 (67.1%) absent from 1.0; 478 (32.9%) present in both sets Primary-Domain Subset The same 22,003 -label baseline 962 labels from primary_victim_domain alone 726 (75.5%) absent from 1.0; 236 (24.5%) present in both sets Recorded Appliance Logins 73,932 login rows; the text does not contain separate privilege or validation fields 1,672 cleartext rows labelled FortiGate_Super_Admin_Verified_Login in the CSV 906 on hosts absent from 1.0; 766 on the 765 overlapping hosts Local-User / SSL-VPN-Related Records This configuration category was not captured 83,414 records, including 37,076 cleartext password fields Account and secret exposure relevant to remote access and local authentication Active Directory LDAP Binds This configuration category was not captured 2,163 records, including 1,576 cleartext bind-password fields Directory service identities, configured servers, and exposed authentication material System Admin Configuration Entries Full administrator configuration tables were not captured 13,786 entries, including 13,369 hash-labelled records and 417 empty secret fields Coexisting administrative identities and account relationships for investigation HA Cluster & SMTP Relay Records These configuration categories were not captured 208 HA records and 176 SMTP records; 144 and 105 , respectively, are labelled cleartext Secret exposure extending to cluster membership and email-server integrations How the comparison was counted Host matching uses the host identifier in each record, without resolving DNS names or treating different ports as different hosts. FortiBleed 1.0 contains 68,709 IPv4 addresses and 346 DNS hostnames ; FortiBleed 2.0 contains 1,665 IPv4 addresses and 24 DNS hostnames . The overlap comprises 744 IP addresses and 21 hostnames . These identifiers are not a count of independently verified physical appliances. The 1.0 total includes 4,041 duplicate lines , leaving 69,891 distinct full rows . Credential matching compares each CSV login with all 1.0 records for the same host, using the exact, case-sensitive username and password. “Verified login” refers to the CSV category, not a fresh authentication test. CSV domain sources: The domain comparison uses only primary_victim_domain , domains extracted from email addresses in fortiguard_or_mssp_id , and domains extracted from email addresses in username . It does not extract domains from user_email , all_public_domains , all_internal_domains , ldap_dn , or any other CSV field. After trimming, lowercasing, and applying the same DNS syntax rule to both datasets, the three sources contribute 962 primary-domain labels , 594 registration-email domains , and 378 username-email domains . These sets overlap; their deduplicated union contains 1,453 labels. The syntax rule requires dot-separated DNS labels and an alphabetic top-level label of at least two characters. Exact subdomains are preserved. No freemail-provider exclusion list, parent-domain collapsing, or live DNS validation is applied. Reading the percentages: 67.1% applies to the three-source union ( 975 / 1,453 ). 75.5% applies only to the primary-domain subset ( 726 / 962 ). Registration and account-email domains can identify providers, freemail services, or other relationships as well as customer organizations. Neither percentage is a count of uniquely identified companies or newly occurring compromises. What the 101,419 Records Contain Empty password fields are account records without a stored secret in this export. Cleartext secret records 40,573 (40.0%) Account records with an empty password field 36,104 (35.6%) Hash-classified records 13,999 (13.8%) Undecrypted FortiOS ENC values 10,743 (10.6%) See the breakdown by account type The account categories and secret classifications reconcile to the same 101,419 records : Account or Configuration Role Total Cleartext Hash-Classified ENC Empty Local users / SSL-VPN/Auth 83,414 37,076 0 10,679 35,659 System Admin configuration entries 13,786 0 13,369 0 417 Active Directory LDAP binds 2,163 1,576 559 0 28 Administrative logins marked verified 1,672 1,672 0 0 0 SMTP email-server accounts 176 105 71 0 0 HA cluster records 208 144 0 64 0 Total 101,419 40,573 13,999 10,743 36,104 The hash-classified total consists of 10,376 SH2 , 2,676 PB2 , 316 AK1 , and 631 records carrying the generic FortiOS_Hash label. The generic label appears on 559 LDAP , 71 SMTP , and 1 System Admin record. These are record counts, not counts of unique people or currently usable credentials. The 36,104 empty password fields include 35,659 local-user , 417 System Admin , and 28 LDAP records; the export does not identify an authentication backend for every such entry. 4. What the 765 Overlapping Hosts Reveal Matching hosts let us compare the administrative access recorded in the two collections. The 765 overlapping host identifiers account for 766 administrator-login rows in FortiBleed 2.0. The comparison reveals both identical credentials and alternative administrator identities. 68.4% Identical Credentials In 524 of the 766 login records , the username and cleartext password match a FortiBleed 1.0 record for the same host. This is a match between recorded credentials; it does not establish an uninterrupted history of access or password reuse between the periods represented by the datasets. 31.6% Different Administrator Identities The remaining 242 records use a different administrator username. In 222 cases , the password also differs; in 20 cases , a different username shares the same password. These records identify additional administrative accounts associated with the same hosts. Recurring Account Patterns In the differing-login cohort, the FortiBleed 1.0 records most frequently list admin (66), Technical_support (22), laboratorio (16), forti-auth-tech (11), and martinwong (7). The corresponding FortiBleed 2.0 logins include: fgtsecure — 106 occurrences, with a recurring password pattern admin — 25 occurrences Technical_support — 22 occurrences callcenter / Callcenter — 17 occurrences fgtsec — 11 , and forticloud-sync — 5 Account Coexistence in 89.3% of Differing-Login Cases In 216 of the 242 comparisons (89.3%) , the administrator username listed in FortiBleed 1.0 also appears in the earlier configuration’s System Admin table, alongside the different login recorded in FortiBleed 2.0. In 26 cases (10.7%) , that username is absent. This finding establishes account coexistence in the earlier material. It cannot establish later account deletion, continuous access, or the outcome of remediation after the FortiBleed 1.0 disclosure. The repeated names and credential patterns give affected organizations a focused set of accounts to check against configuration history and ownership records. Names such as admin and callcenter alone do not establish that an account is unauthorized. 5. Behind the Registration Email The email address used to register a firewall may belong to the company managing it, rather than the organization whose network it protects. MSSPs, telecommunications providers, and IT contractors can therefore appear in a perimeter dataset in place of their customers. A personal email address or NONE registration offers even less context. The three selected fields provide complementary clues: the CSV’s primary attribution, the email domain used for FortiGuard registration, and email domains appearing in usernames. Across the 765 matching host identifiers , their combined values supply at least one domain label absent from that host’s 1.0 registration-email domains on 462 hosts (60.4%) . These are additional domain relationships to investigate; they are not all newly identified victim organizations. Figure 2: The CSV records jp.ricoh.com as the FortiGuard registration-email domain and elumax.com in primary_victim_domain . These fields describe different relationships to the appliance. The configuration excerpt illustrates the underlying registration and directory context. Recorded Host Registration Domain in 1.0 Configuration Attribution in 2.0 Evidence in the Supplied Records 203.159.253.220 nti.co.th — IT contractor ovec.go.th — Thailand’s Office of the Vocational Education Commission The CSV’s primary_victim_domain identifies ovec.go.th , while the registration-email domain is nti.co.th . The CSV contains 22 local-user records for this host. 211.75.64.189 jp.ricoh.com — Ricoh Japan elumax.com — Elumax Corporation The CSV records the registration-email domain jp.ricoh.com and primary attribution elumax.com . 49.229.69.162 dataworkconnect.com — IT vendor ads.payap.ac.th — Payap University The CSV records ads.payap.ac.th in primary_victim_domain and dataworkconnect.com as the registration-email domain. How the attribution difference was counted For each matching host, the comparison forms a deduplicated union from the same three CSV sources used in Section 3: primary_victim_domain , email domains in fortiguard_or_mssp_id , and email domains in username . It compares that union with all FortiGuard registration-email domains recorded for the host in 1.0. A host counts once if it has any additional valid domain label. This yields 462 hosts with additional labels, 244 with only matching labels, and 59 with no usable label from these sources. Of the 462, 256 also have a matching label, and two have no registration-email domain in 1.0. The result measures additional domain information, not a change in ownership or a count of newly compromised organizations. 6. The Network Details Inside the Backup A directory bind record can reveal both an account and the server it connects to. In this export, ldap_server , ldap_dn , device hostnames, and trusted-host fields add context that a perimeter login list lacks. These details help defenders connect an exposed credential to the internal service that depends on it. A full FortiGate backup can go further. Address objects, policies, and static routes can identify backup systems, hypervisor-management interfaces, directory servers, and other internal assets. Assessing those additional exposures requires the full policy, address-object, and routing tables. The credential export examined here contains the LDAP and host metadata, so affected organizations should review the underlying configuration as part of their investigation. Identity infrastructure: Reconcile exposed LDAP server addresses and bind identities with directory services and review their access history. Management access: Review administrator profiles, trusted hosts, and the services reachable from the appliance. Backup and virtualization systems: Inspect the full configuration for relevant address objects, access policies, and routes, then assess whether the exposed identities could reach those systems. Read MFA Fields as Recorded The local-user records contain 5,042 recognized MFA-method values : 4,114 fortitoken , 909 email , 18 fortitoken-cloud , and one sms . Another 78,369 entries have a blank two_fa field, and three contain anomalous values. A blank field is missing information, not an explicit disabled setting. Effective protection must be assessed against the appliance and any external identity-provider or RADIUS policies. 7. What Affected Organizations Should Check The response should cover the appliance, its administrator accounts, the secrets stored in its configuration, and any internal activity those credentials may have enabled. Begin by comparing the affected records with current settings and the changes made since the exposure. That establishes which risks remain relevant and which have already been addressed. Apply the appropriate firmware updates and restrict management access. Fortinet’s response guidance also calls for session termination, credential resets, configuration review, and investigation of potential lateral movement. The configuration findings give that review four concrete areas of focus: 1. Review Administrator Accounts Compare config system admin with approved ownership, configuration history, and logs. Investigate recurring names such as fgtsecure , fgtsec , Technical_support , forticloud-sync , and forti-auth-tech . Remove accounts confirmed to be unauthorized. Other names identified in the original analysis include callcenter , my_admin , districtadmin , ftadm1n , and super_admin . A name is an investigation lead; account ownership and history establish whether it belongs. 2. Review Directory Bind Secrets Identify the service accounts configured under config user ldap . Check whether their secrets were replaced after the exposure, rotate any still-relevant exposed values, and update dependent services. Remove unnecessary privileges, including excessive Domain Admins membership, and inspect authentication activity. The 1,576 cleartext bind records are a concrete starting point; the sensitivity of each account depends on its permissions. 3. Review VPN Access and MFA Review config user local , VPN policies, and external authentication dependencies. Reset exposed local secrets that remain relevant and disable unused accounts. Verify effective MFA across administrative and remote-access paths. The export includes 35,659 local-user records with empty password fields ; assess those identities at the appropriate authentication source without assuming that an empty field identifies a particular backend or MFA state. 4. Review HA, RADIUS, and SMTP Secrets Review cluster credentials under config system ha , RADIUS shared secrets, and email-server credentials under config system email-server . Coordinate any replacements with the services that use them. The CSV contains 208 HA records, including 144 cleartext secrets , and 176 SMTP records, including 105 cleartext secrets . Account for these integrations alongside firewall and directory access. Data sources, counting rules, and chronology Source inventory: FortiBleed 1.0 was checked against all_fortinet.txt ; FortiBleed 2.0 was checked against the supplied combined credential CSV. The 1.0 text contains 73,932 login rows , including 4,041 exact duplicate rows and 486 blank-password fields . The earlier 73,931 count omitted one record prefixed with a byte-order marker. There are 69,055 host identifiers : 68,709 IPv4 addresses and 346 DNS hostnames . The text has no independent role, verification-result, or timestamp field. Configuration export: The CSV has 101,419 rows , including eight exact duplicate rows , across 1,703 source files . Its 1,689 nonempty host identifiers comprise 1,665 IPv4 addresses and 24 hostnames . One source file, containing 15 rows , has no host identifier; 13 hosts appear in two source files each. File counts, record counts, and physical-device counts are different units. Verification labels: All 1,672 administrative-login-category rows are marked Verified_Active_Login in the CSV. Of these, 1,633 explicitly have accprofile=super_admin ; 39 have another or blank profile. These are source labels, not fresh authentication tests or a statement of present-day access. Dates: Populated report_date fields cover 1,672 files / 98,971 records and all fall on February 20, 2026 . Another 31 files / 2,448 records are undated. These timestamps date the reports represented in the export. The approximate February versus likely May/June chronology reflects the investigation’s current understanding of the material; individual compromise, extraction, acquisition, and disclosure dates are separate events. Interpretation: The analysis concerns recorded exposure. Account names, source status labels, recovered secrets, and attribution fields need to be evaluated alongside an organization’s own records. The files alone do not establish successful internal compromise, continuous attacker access, or the outcome of later remediation. Check Your Organization in Cavalier & the Free FortiBleed Portal Hudson Rock has indexed the 101,419 FortiBleed 2.0 credential and account records alongside FortiBleed 1.0 in Cavalier . Use the free domain lookup to identify relevant exposure records, then compare the findings with your organization’s inventory, account ownership, and response history. For Hudson Rock Data Enrichment customers: The raw FortiBleed 2.0, FortiBleed 1.0, and LiteLLM datasets are available through Cavalier’s Breach Data hub. What impacted organizations receive in their ethical disclosure: Exact Appliance IP & Hostname: Recorded appliance identifiers to reconcile with your historical inventory. Exposed Usernames & Hashes: Recorded System Admin accounts, recurring accounts requiring review ( fgtsecure , etc.), and recovered local-user credentials. Active Directory LDAP Bind Account Exposure: The recorded service account name and any recovered cleartext password associated with your appliance. Internal Network Metadata: Available internal network metadata, including LDAP server addresses and directory-domain references. Figure 3: Overview of Hudson Rock’s free FortiBleed lookup portal ( hudsonrock.com/fortinet ), covering both datasets and allowing organizations to query affected domains and request their ethical disclosure. Figure 4: Cavalier’s Breach Data menu provides Hudson Rock Data Enrichment customers with access to the FortiBleed 1.0, FortiBleed 2.0, and LiteLLM datasets. Figure 5: Cavalier displays 54 credential and account records associated with bangkok.go.th across two hosts . The export includes two logins marked verified in the source, alongside configuration records and attribution details. item.title: [Articles | InfoStealers] 38,628 Crypto Orders. 10,139 IPs. What Wagyu’s Alleged Leak Means for Monero Privacy.
item.description: HR HUDSON ROCK / INFOSTEALERS.COM Threat Intelligence  •  October 28, 2026 Research / Cryptocurrency privacy 38,628 Crypto Orders. 10,139 IPs. What Wagyu’s Alleged Leak Means for Monero Privacy. Monero’s cryptography was not broken. Yet the records connect its users to public-chain activity — and include seven-figure transaction clusters marked with alleged hacker, theft and mixer attributions. Hudson Rock Research Wagyu.xyz 15-minute read Original dataset analysis Can Monero users be traced through a hacked exchange? Not by magically decrypting Monero’s blockchain. But potentially by reading what a swap service knows before coins ever enter the privacy network — and what it records when those coins leave. That is the central finding of Hudson Rock’s review of purported Wagyu.xyz transaction data supplied alongside a WhiteArmor-associated claim. The files contain order histories, cryptocurrency destinations, transaction identifiers, connection metadata and an IP-level activity index. They do not demonstrate an attack on the Monero protocol, and their alleged breach provenance has not been independently authenticated. 38,628 Total order records in orders.csv 10,139 Distinct IP addresses, not confirmed individuals 8,137 Orders naming a native XMR receiving address 4,580 Completed cross-chain-to-XMR records joining deposit TX, address and IP Hudson Rock calculations from the provided CSVs; records span July 18–October 26, 2026. An order is not necessarily a completed trade, and an IP address is not necessarily a customer. 01 / THE INCIDENT CLAIM WhiteArmor’s claim raises a different question than its ransom note. On October 27–28, 2026, ransomware-tracking services indexed WhiteArmor listings naming Wagyu.xyz , including a second entry called “wagyu.xyz unfairness.” The associated text concentrates on alleged unfair coin-flip odds and undisclosed swap fees. Its accusations are not proof of intrusion, ransomware deployment or financial misconduct, and Hudson Rock has not independently verified how the supplied files were obtained. Wagyu presents itself as a no-KYC route between Monero (XMR), other cryptocurrencies and cross-chain infrastructure. Its service records therefore sit at a particularly sensitive boundary: a transparent blockchain on one side and a privacy-preserving cryptocurrency on the other. A leak at that boundary can expose relationships that Monero deliberately keeps off its public chain. The security story isn’t “Monero has been cracked.” It is that a service handling private-coin conversions may preserve an off-chain ledger linking customers’ requests, public-chain movements, private-coin destinations and connection metadata. 02 / THE PRIVACY GAP The blockchain hides the destination. The swap order records it. Monero uses stealth addresses, ring signatures and Ring Confidential Transactions to hide recipients, sender relationships and amounts in its on-chain records. A normal public observer cannot take an XMR receiving address and search the chain for a complete history of incoming and outgoing transfers. But a swap service still has to know where to send funds. When a customer requests BTC → XMR, it may store the Bitcoin deposit transaction, the intended Monero receiving address, the order amount, the submission time, the client IP and the session used to track the order. Those values appear together in the supplied records. How an off-chain order links information that public XMR transactions do not Transparent chain BTC / ETH / SOL deposit Deposit address · transaction hash · asset and value → The sensitive junction Wagyu order record IP address · timestamp · session ID · browser headers · order mapping → Privacy chain Native XMR destination Receiving address supplied to the service · internal payout status A link in a service database is not evidence that Monero’s hidden sender, recipient or amount has become public on-chain. We isolated 8,137 records with a native-XMR destination format and Monero output chain identifier; 6,692 were marked completed. Within the completed cross-chain subset, 4,580 records contained an incoming deposit transaction hash, a Monero receiving address and a client IP in the same row. Among these were 1,011 completed BTC → XMR orders with that linkage. A real BTC → XMR record, deliberately redacted Supplied CSV / September 2026 Order type Bitcoin → native XMR Recorded status Completed Client IP 103.75.xxx.xxx Transaction size $1,000–$5,000 band BTC deposit transaction Recorded / hash withheld XMR destination Recorded / address withheld Browser information Recorded Session identifier Recorded / withheld Based on an actual completed row. Amounts are grouped, timestamps are reduced to the month, IP octets are masked, and complete wallet addresses, hashes, order IDs and session IDs are intentionally withheld to avoid reproducing a targetable user-level record. This establishes that the supplied application data can map a public-chain deposit to an XMR destination and a network connection . It does not establish the customer’s legal identity, prove that the requestor owns the receiving wallet or reveal where any XMR later moves. 03 / TWO-WAY CORRELATION It works in reverse, too: XMR can become visible again at the exit. The more consequential angle is not limited to buying Monero. We found 11,317 native-XMR-input swap records containing a 95-character Monero deposit address and a destination for another asset. Of those, 9,187 completed records also retained an outgoing transaction hash in the corresponding order data. For an XMR → ETH transaction, for example, the service can connect the private-coin deposit it accepted to the Ethereum address it paid, alongside IP and timing information. That destination can then be examined on Ethereum’s transparent blockchain. Crucially, the service’s XMR deposit address is not proof of which Monero wallet originally funded it; Monero does not disclose that sender relationship publicly. Putting both directions together reveals the real exposure: entry and exit metadata can erode pseudonymity even while the private blockchain continues doing its job. It is a correlation problem, not an XMR decryption problem. Privacy can survive on-chain and still fail in the database sitting next to the chain. 04 / THE SECOND CSV 10,139 IPs — and an activity map extending beyond individual swaps. The companion file, users_wagyu.csv , is particularly informative. It groups activity by IP, providing an order count, number of distinct destinations, first and last observation, risk values, reported countries and network-provider classifications. We matched its 10,139 IP-level entries against orders.csv : each one corresponds to an IP in the larger file, and the per-IP order totals reconcile exactly. This is not a verified database of 10,139 unique human users. Shared IPs, corporate NAT, VPN servers, Tor exit nodes, hosting services and automated API traffic can represent multiple unrelated people — while one person can use several IPs. 1,328 IP addresses appear in both XMR-output orders and orders delivering other assets. 130 Repeated session IDs span more than one IP address in the order export. 261 XMR receiving addresses occur in orders submitted from more than one IP. These are correlation opportunities, not proof of shared ownership . A reused session ID can be more informative than an IP alone, but it may belong to a shared integration or automated workflow. Likewise, a popular destination can be a custodial wallet rather than one individual. The network labels themselves include Tor, VPN, hosting and ISP categories. The mere presence of an IP beside a trade does not reveal the person’s home address, and a country or routing code should not be treated as verified geography. 05 / HIGH-VALUE TRANSACTION LEADS Hacker labels, seven-figure Monero orders and some revealing connections. The data contains another striking finding: some large Monero-related orders carry source labels such as “Poloniex Hacker,” “DCENT Wallet Hacker,” “Theft” and “Tornado.Cash: 100 ETH.” Even without knowing who controlled the wallets, the records preserve the source and destination addresses that Wagyu associated with those orders. What these findings do — and do not — establish. The labels come from the supplied Wagyu records. We have verified the order counts, amounts and relationships within those files, but have not independently established that any wallet belongs to a known hacker or that its funds were laundered. The dollar figures are values recorded by Wagyu for completed orders, not independently verified stolen proceeds. Case 01 / Source label: “Poloniex Hacker” Six Monero bridge withdrawals totaling $1.03 million. $1,025,047 October 11–12, 2026 · Recorded order value The export contains six completed XMR bridge withdrawals marked “Poloniex Hacker.” All six share the same recorded source address, Monero receiving address and session identifier. They were submitted from two different IP addresses. 6 Completed withdrawals 1 Shared Monero destination 2 Recorded IP addresses The November 2023 Poloniex hack is publicly documented. However, we have not confirmed that this source address was involved. These records show bridge withdrawals into native XMR; they do not contain the incoming transaction hashes needed to establish the funds’ earlier history. Case 02 / Source label: “DCENT Wallet Hacker” Three Ethereum-to-Monero orders linked by one source wallet. $902,627 October 13, 2026 · Three completed orders Two completed orders totaling $651,667 carry the label “DCENT Wallet Hacker.” A third, worth $250,960, has no such label, but shares the same Ethereum depositor address, Monero destination and recorded IP. Taken together, the three orders represent approximately $903,000 in recorded swap volume. 2 Orders carrying the label 1 Additional linked order 1 Shared Monero destination D’CENT publicly reported unauthorized App Wallet transfers in September 2026 . This provides context for the name, not proof that the three Wagyu orders contained those stolen assets. Two orders are also marked as restricted in the export despite a completed status; determining whether those flags existed before or after execution would require the platform’s screening logs. Case 03 / Two source labels, one Monero destination “Theft” and Tornado Cash-labeled orders converge within an hour. $823,397 September 25, 2026 · Seven completed orders Seven completed orders identify two different Ethereum depositor addresses and the same recorded XMR receiving address within roughly 58 minutes. Two orders carry the label “Theft” and total $559,107. Five are labeled “Tornado.Cash: 100 ETH” and total $264,290. All seven orders also share a recorded IP address, masked here as 146.70.xxx.xxx . A shared destination is a useful investigative connection, although it does not prove the wallets had the same human owner. Shared infrastructure, custodial wallets or automated services can produce similar patterns. 2 Ethereum source addresses 1 Shared Monero destination ~58 min First-to-last order interval A Tornado Cash association is not inherently evidence of laundering. The five mixer-labeled orders described here also appear in the broader 25-order group below. Case 04 / Source label: “Theft” One depositor, 360 Monero orders and unusually consistent amounts. $1,720,820 September 17–October 17, 2026 A single Ethereum depositor address labeled “Theft” appears in 360 completed Monero-output orders, sent to 13 different XMR destinations. Most of the orders are remarkably similar in size: 315 fall between $4,900 and $5,100. The records span 20 IP addresses, and 354 orders retain incoming transaction hashes. 360 Completed orders 315 Orders near $5,000 13 Monero destinations The repetition makes this a worthwhile transaction-pattern investigation. It might reflect deliberate order splitting, but it could equally result from an automated trading workflow, route capacity or limits imposed by the service. The amounts alone cannot establish an attempt to evade financial controls. Case 05 / Source label: “Tornado.Cash: 100 ETH” A wider group totals $3.56 million in recorded ETH-to-XMR swaps. $3,561,386 25 completed orders · Recorded order value Across the full dataset, 25 completed Ethereum-to-Monero orders carry the label “Tornado.Cash: 100 ETH.” They involve four source addresses and four Monero receiving addresses. A single source-to-destination pair accounts for 12 orders worth approximately $2.03 million, placed over about two hours on October 3, 2026. 25 Completed ETH-to-XMR orders 4 Source addresses 4 Monero destinations Five of these 25 orders are already counted in Case 03. The $3.56 million therefore overlaps with the $823,397 case; the figures should not be added together. Mixer usage is not evidence of criminal conduct on its own. Why these records matter for investigations. For investigators, the value lies in linking the data points: a source-chain address, a service order, a Monero receiving address and the metadata recorded at the time. Some apparent relationships span multiple transactions, different labels or repeated destinations. Those connections give investigators leads to verify against independent blockchain evidence and other records. They do not reveal transfers made after the funds enter Monero, nor do they identify the individuals who control the wallets. The case totals are recorded order values, may include the same funds moving more than once, and are not a cumulative estimate of money laundering or stolen assets. 06 / THE RETENTION QUESTION One overlooked field may be the most uncomfortable: userDeletedAt . Among the supplied records, 4,002 completed orders contain a populated field literally called userDeletedAt . Those same rows are still present in the export. All 4,002 retain an IP and destination; 3,180 also include a deposit transaction hash. We cannot determine from the field name alone exactly what deletion operation occurred, what the site’s retention policy promised, or whether these rows came from a historical backup. So this is not proof of an unlawful failure to erase data . It is evidence that the supplied dataset still holds sensitive transaction metadata for records marked with a user-deletion timestamp. Why this matters: A privacy interface can make a transaction disappear from a user’s account view without necessarily removing the underlying connection between their IP, trade and destination from every operational record or backup. 07 / FACT-CHECK Can this data actually be used to trace XMR users? Yes, in a defined and limited sense. Here is the boundary between what the files demonstrate and what they do not. Question Assessment Why Can a public-chain payment be linked to an XMR receiving address? Supported in data Completed cross-chain order rows record deposit transaction hash, XMR destination, client IP and timestamp together. Can an XMR-to-crypto exit be linked to a transparent payout address? Supported in data XMR-input orders retain service deposit addresses and destination addresses, often with an outgoing transaction hash. Can network and session metadata help correlate activity? Supported in data The IP rollup and reused session IDs create off-chain associations, subject to VPN, NAT and automation ambiguity. Can the files alone identify the human behind an IP? Not established IPs, wallet addresses and request headers are not reliable proof of a legal identity or a single user. Can an analyst follow subsequent XMR transfers on Monero? Not demonstrated Monero conceals on-chain sender, recipient and amount relationships; this dataset does not defeat that protection. Does this establish who originally sent XMR to a service deposit address? Not demonstrated An operator-issued deposit address is not the originator’s wallet, and a private Monero input cannot be attributed from the address alone. The labeled high-value transaction clusters described above illustrate the investigative uses of these records, but the labels are not independently verified claims about criminal proceeds. A cross-chain transaction plus IP metadata can become an investigative lead. Identification may be possible when independently corroborated with exchange KYC data, lawful provider records or other reliable evidence. Without corroboration, it remains a lead — not an identification. 08 / THE SECURITY ANGLE For criminals, the off-chain metadata may be more useful than blockchain tracing. Exact trade context makes targeted social engineering far more credible. A criminal holding an order’s real amount, approximate time, asset pair and payout destination could construct a believable fake refund or support message. A large historical conversion could also become the basis of financial profiling or extortion. These are plausible abuse cases; we have not established that any has occurred. What a criminal could attempt Transaction-aware phishing: cite a real swap to impersonate support or demand a “recovery” payment. Cross-chain wallet clustering: connect public-chain activity to the same service session or network source. Targeted extortion: use historic transaction values and timing to suggest knowledge of a person’s finances. Dataset enrichment: compare exposed metadata with other compromised records to search for corroborating identity clues. Where infostealers fit in Infostealer malware can expose browser activity, saved credentials, session artifacts and cryptocurrency-related information on an infected endpoint. In an entirely separate dataset, those artifacts may sometimes add context to a pseudonymous exchange order. No supplied evidence indicates that infostealers caused this alleged Wagyu incident, or that Hudson Rock matched any Wagyu customer to an infostealer infection. The risk is a general correlation mechanism, not a finding about specific users. 09 / WHAT THE ACTOR CLAIMS The allegations about hidden fees and rigged games need a separate audit. The WhiteArmor-associated text alleges undisclosed swap fees and manipulated coin-flip odds. The accompanying configuration snapshot does distinguish public and “hidden” fee tiers, while an example order contains discrepant quoted, fee and later adjustment fields. Those findings warrant investigation, but a snapshot or attacker calculation alone does not prove an intentional scheme or the exact amount of customer losses. The attached aggregate fee summary covers 28,840 completed swap/bridge orders , a subset that reconciles to completed order counts in the larger CSV. Yet the summary records 11,098 orders in its over category, whereas the actor’s note alleges 13,190 above the quoted rate. Likewise, the note’s coin-flip outcome imbalance does not by itself establish statistical rigging. We have therefore not adopted its claims of “proven” fraud as fact. There is a further reason not to manufacture a spectacular dollar-volume figure from orders.csv : several expired orders contain implausibly huge amountUsd values. This article reports record counts and verified field co-occurrence rather than summing every row into a misleading trading-volume estimate. 10 / RECOMMENDATIONS What users and privacy-focused platforms should take from this. For users Assume a swap provider may retain source and destination addresses, amounts, timestamps and connection metadata, even without an account or KYC. Be skeptical of unsolicited refund, recovery or verification messages that reference a real historic order. Avoid unnecessarily sharing transaction IDs or linking wallet addresses to public profiles. VPN or Tor use can limit direct-IP exposure but cannot erase information intentionally submitted to the service. If you believe your order information was exposed, check announcements through a known authentic channel; do not enter recovery phrases or private keys into support links. For exchanges and bridges Minimize how long IP addresses, session identifiers, destination addresses and order mappings are retained together. Separate high-sensitivity transaction data from operational telemetry; implement least privilege, encryption and audited access. Explain what “delete” means across live systems, logs, analytics exports and backups; verify actual retention controls. Build incident response around the linkage between records, not merely the presence of standalone wallet addresses. 11 / THE TAKEAWAY Monero can keep a secret that the service around it does not. Our analysis does not show a vulnerability in Monero’s cryptography. It shows that a purported exchange order dataset contains enough off-chain information to connect thousands of privacy-coin transactions to source-chain movements, destination addresses, IPs and sessions. The records can support meaningful correlation; they cannot, on their own, name users or follow hidden XMR transfers. For any company selling financial privacy, metadata retention is part of the threat model. A “no-KYC” transaction can still leave a remarkably detailed trail — and that trail may survive long after the user thinks the transaction has disappeared. METHODOLOGY & SOURCES How we verified the numbers and limited the claims. We analyzed the supplied orders.csv (38,628 rows; 45 columns), the users_wagyu.csv IP-level summary (10,139 rows), the WhiteArmor-associated note, and supporting configuration, fee and coin-flip files. We reconciled IP order counts, isolated native XMR address formats and order kinds, checked completion status and counted field co-occurrence. The IP-summary export has a misaligned network-classification header, which we accounted for during inspection. For the high-value case studies, we filtered to completed rows, grouped by recorded source and destination fields, checked source labels and shared wallet identifiers, and summed recorded USD values per group. Named labels describe the export, not externally verified wallet attributions; linked orders and group totals overlap. The datasets’ origin, completeness and authenticity are not independently established. We did not independently verify blockchain settlement, identify private individuals, publish full wallet addresses, transaction hashes, order IDs or IPs, or attempt to follow Monero transactions. “Completed” means the export labels an order as completed, not independently verified settlement. The publication of a ransomware-group listing is a claim, not proof of encryption or exfiltration. Public incident context: Wagyu.xyz / WhiteArmor listing, October 27 ; “Wagyu.xyz unfairness” listing, October 28 ; HackerFeeds reporting methodology . Context for incident names appearing in unverified source labels: The Block: November 2023 Poloniex hack ; DCENT: September 17, 2026 official incident report . These sources document the external incidents, not a verified match between their stolen funds and any wallet in the supplied dataset. Monero technical references: Official Monero FAQ ; Stealth addresses ; Network and IP privacy considerations . Figures are from Hudson Rock’s analysis of supplied material, not independent confirmations from Wagyu. WhiteArmor’s financial accusations are presented as allegations, not proven findings. No personally identifying raw records are republished. HUDSON ROCK RESEARCH Threat intelligence and the cybercrime ecosystem Infostealers.com   ·   October 28, 2026 The post 38,628 Crypto Orders. 10,139 IPs. What Wagyu’s Alleged Leak Means for Monero Privacy. appeared first on InfoStealers .

item.title: [Articles | InfoStealers] Polymarket Breach Alert: Wallet-Draining Code Found in a Third-Party Script
item.description: HUDSON ROCK INFOSTEALERS.COM · THREAT RESEARCH Developing investigation Polymarket / Third-party JavaScript Polymarket Breach Alert: Wallet-Draining Code Found in a Third-Party Script A script associated with performance monitoring contains code to access trading sessions, sell positions, and redirect assets. Polymarket’s own production build records the integration’s removal. By Hudson Rock Research October 29, 2026 Evidence timestamps in UTC The payload Polymarket-specific theft logic Reads account context and seeks the page’s existing trading client and signer. The corroboration Removal recorded in a live build A production asset explicitly names removal of the DebugBear RUM script. Recipient-address holdings $2.19 million displayed The supplied screenshot shows substantial holdings at the payload’s fallback recipient address. Aggregate losses remain unverified. A performance-monitoring integration should measure how quickly a page loads. The JavaScript Hudson Rock retrieved from a DebugBear URL associated with Polymarket does something far more consequential: it searches for a logged-in user’s trading client, inspects their portfolio, and attempts to sell or transfer their assets. [1] On October 29, 2026, we independently downloaded the file identified in a community warning and reviewed it as text. Two downloads returned the same 15,187-byte payload. We also found a separate artifact in Polymarket’s published application code: production build metadata containing the change message “chore(polymarket): remove debugbear rum script (#15337)” , with a build timestamp of 17:59:20 UTC that evening. [1] [2] A supplied PolygonScan screenshot shows more than $2 million in holdings at the address embedded in the payload as its fallback recipient. The matching address links the screenshot to the script, but the balance is not a verified total of stolen funds. The number of affected users, aggregate losses attributable to this incident, and the initial compromise mechanism remain unresolved. [11] What is established Malicious asset-theft logic was present in the retrieved file, and Polymarket’s served build records removal of the DebugBear integration. Our later homepage snapshot did not contain the suspect script reference. This supports removal in the observed build; it does not establish the exact exposure window or certify every existing browser session safe. The warning that led to the payload The evidence supplied to Hudson Rock includes a screenshot of a message attributed to a user named Vivian. It identifies cdn.debugbear[.]com/C7xcKKrjUnXK.js and alleges that the file accesses login credentials, triggers wallet signatures, sells holdings, and transfers assets. The message also says its author retrieved the same content and hash more than once. [3] Supplied evidence. The screenshot identifies the exact script examined in this investigation. Its visible time is 7:57 PM; no date, time zone, server identity, sample, or hash value is visible. The screenshot’s authorship and original posting context were not independently authenticated. We tested the central technical allegation by retrieving that exact URL. At 18:12:06 UTC , it returned JavaScript containing the behavior described below. A repeat retrieval at 18:13:04 UTC returned identical bytes. This establishes repeatability for our captures; it cannot establish that our copy matches the unseen hash referenced in the screenshot. [1] A separately published WhoGetsMyData scan dated October 29 records Polymarket loading the same script URL and permitting its host in the page’s Content Security Policy. We could review the publicly indexed report, but could not retrieve its underlying evidence files. It corroborates the integration’s presence; we cannot compare the script bytes it received with our captured sample. [4] The financial evidence: millions at the recipient address The supplied PolygonScan screenshot identifies 0x3F99139F1C5854bb628c2e576Aaf638e99dFfc18 . This is the same address hard-coded into the retrieved script as its fallback recipient. At the time of the screenshot, its overview shows $2,178,191.78 in POL and a separate $16,170.39 in token holdings . Those two displayed values sum to approximately $2.19 million . [1] [11] Recipient-address balance snapshot. The address matches the script’s embedded fallback recipient. The POL and token-holdings panels show approximately $2.19 million combined. A separate multichain widget displays $2,163,862.69; it is not an additional balance to add. The screenshot’s capture time and valuation differences between widgets are not established. Select the image to inspect the figures. This is evidence of substantial holdings at an address explicitly selected by the payload. It is not a verified accounting of the proceeds of this incident: establishing that would require tracing the source and timing of individual transfers. It reaches for the trading session already inside the page The most revealing feature is the way the payload looks for authority. It searches the application already running in the browser for the objects needed to place orders and request signatures. Its target is the user’s active Polymarket session. [1] 1. Read the account’s authentication context The script reads three local-storage entries: polymarket.auth.params , polymarket.auth.proxyWallet , and poly_clob_api_key_map . These provide authorization context, the deposit-wallet address, and a map of CLOB API credentials. The code distinguishes between eoa and magic account types and checks for account and credential data before continuing. [1] The distinction between access and exfiltration matters here. The sample reads credential-related material, but our review did not identify a routine that sends the credential map, a password, a seed phrase, or a private key to its reporting endpoint. Its central approach is to reuse authority already available in the authenticated application. 2. Find the live trading client The code traverses React’s internal component structures, looking through component properties and hook state for an object with trading methods such as postOrder and createOrder or createMarketOrder . Once found, it attempts to use that object and its signer. This is application-specific logic aimed directly at Polymarket’s trading workflow. [1] The payload searches for the trading machinery the user has already authorized and tries to use it to move their assets. Polymarket’s documentation distinguishes API-request authentication from wallet authorization: CLOB API credentials authenticate private requests, while placing an order also requires a wallet signature. The payload’s search for the live client and signer is therefore a significant part of its design. [6] 3. Inspect the portfolio and choose a path The script queries balances and positions, calculates a portfolio value, and applies configurable thresholds. Its fallback configuration uses a total-value threshold of 10 and a per-position threshold of 10. It also checks Polymarket’s geoblock response and exits if the response marks the visitor as blocked. These are selection conditions visible in the code, not measurements of the affected population. [1] EOA branch Transfer position tokens For eligible positions, the code builds an ERC-1155 batch transfer to the configured recipient. Magic / non-EOA branch Attempt sales, then move balances The code submits SELL orders at increasingly aggressive prices and then attempts to transfer available proceeds. This branching means that “the script sells everyone’s holdings” would be inaccurate. One path attempts to move the position tokens themselves. Both paths are designed to redirect value, but their success depends on the account state, signer, trading responses, and transaction execution. 4. Request signatures and submit transfers The payload constructs EIP-712 DepositWallet batch messages for Polygon, requests signatures through the existing signer, and attempts to submit the signed batches to Polymarket’s relayer. Balance handling includes conversion and swap routes, with a direct token-transfer fallback. [1] Polymarket documents signed batches as a normal mechanism for authorizing deposit-wallet actions; the dangerous element here is the untrusted code selecting the actions and recipient. [7] A signing request is not proof of a silent signature or a completed theft. A provider may prompt, reject, or apply session-specific authorization rules. We did not connect a wallet or execute the sample. The payload’s own success checks also accept some pending relayer states, which cannot independently establish blockchain settlement. 5. Report wallet data and attempted outcomes The sample constructs requests to data.debugbear[.]com containing wallet addresses, IP and country information, operating system, account type, portfolio values, position summaries, and transfer-result fields. Its paths include /metrics/submit , /metrics/update , and /metrics/handle . [1] DebugBear’s own documentation identifies its CDN and data host as parts of legitimate monitoring infrastructure. Their names alone are not evidence of malice. The decisive evidence is the retrieved file’s trading, signing, recipient-selection, and transfer logic. That behavior does not belong in a page-performance measurement script. [5] Polymarket’s own build records the removal Our unauthenticated homepage capture at 18:12:06 UTC did not contain the DebugBear filename or a DebugBear allowance in the returned Content Security Policy. We then inspected all 102 first-party JavaScript files explicitly listed in that response, as inert text. The only DebugBear match was production build metadata describing its removal. [1] [2] Published field Observed value Environment production Change message chore(polymarket): remove debugbear rum script (#15337) Build timestamp 2026-10-29T17:59:20.443Z Commit identifier f908fe564ea73067b09ab1f0c5d683970020fbca This is corroborating technical evidence, rather than a formal incident statement. A build timestamp does not establish the exact moment of deployment or complete containment. Previously opened tabs, cached responses, authenticated pages, and dynamically imported code are outside the scope of this homepage snapshot. A timeline of what can actually be dated All times below are UTC on October 29, 2026 . The screenshot’s undated 7:57 PM display and the script server’s Last-Modified header are not used to infer when an attack began. 17:59:20 Timestamp embedded in Polymarket’s production build metadata for the change removing the DebugBear RUM script. This is a build time, not a verified containment time. [2] 18:12:06 Our first retrieval of the named CDN file returns the 15,187-byte payload. A separate homepage retrieval shows no direct DebugBear script reference. [1] 18:13:04 A second download returns byte-for-byte identical JavaScript and the same SHA-256 hash. [1] 18:13:43 We retrieve the first-party application asset containing the removal message and production build timestamp. [2] What remains unknown The retrieved sample supports describing the file as wallet-draining code . Its author implemented account discovery, asset selection, signing requests, and transfers to a designated recipient. However, static analysis does not establish the effectiveness of every code path. We also found a balance-polling comparison that compares a newly assigned value with itself, illustrating why an intended workflow cannot be treated as a successful one. [1] The additional screenshots show withdrawal activity and a substantial balance at the matching recipient address. We have not independently established the number of affected users, the total losses attributable to this incident, a transaction-by-transaction victim-to-recipient flow, the first malicious delivery, or the initial compromise mechanism. The evidence does not identify an attacker or demonstrate a wider compromise affecting other DebugBear customers. No current incident statement from Polymarket or DebugBear was independently verified during this review. A separate incident: June 25, 2026 Previously published reports of approximately $3 million stolen and a Polymarket reimbursement promise relate to a June 25 incident . The original announcement is dated June 25. Those figures and reimbursement assurances concern the June incident and do not establish the impact or response to the October 29 findings. [10] What users and defenders should do For potentially exposed users Reject unexpected signing and approval requests. Do not approve a message or transaction merely because it appears while a familiar site is open. Close potentially exposed tabs and review activity through a trusted route. Check recent orders, position movements, and wallet transactions using a clean session or independently accessed explorer. Retain timestamps and transaction hashes for any anomaly. Review sessions, API credentials, and permissions with the platform’s support guidance. Disconnecting a wallet does not reverse completed transfers or automatically revoke on-chain approvals. Avoid “recovery” links sent by unsolicited accounts, and never provide a seed phrase. For application and incident-response teams Preserve the delivery evidence. Capture the exact response bytes, hashes, HTTP metadata, loader references, and browser request history before a changing CDN response obscures the exposure window. Review third-party execution on sensitive pages. Remove unnecessary integrations from authenticated trading and signing flows. Investigate exact payloads and request paths; a legitimate vendor hostname alone is an unreliable maliciousness test. Constrain and verify executable dependencies. Where assets can be pinned, Subresource Integrity lets the browser reject unexpected file contents. Pair it with a restrictive Content Security Policy and a controlled update process; simply allowing a trusted CDN does not verify the bytes it serves. [9] Audit the signer boundary. Review what an authenticated page can request, which actions demand fresh user confirmation, and whether untrusted page code can reach the signing interface. Tie remediation to the affected sessions and authorizations actually established by the investigation. Indicators and evidence for defenders These indicators describe the captured sample. The domains are genuine service infrastructure; the file hash, precise paths, and associated behavior provide the stronger detection context. No address below is presented as proof of a quantified theft. Indicator Value and interpretation Captured script cdn.debugbear[.]com/C7xcKKrjUnXK.js Exact URL named in the warning and independently retrieved. File size 15,187 bytes in both captured responses. item.title: [Data Breach] Capcom Data Breach Exposes 11.7 Million Email Addresses
item.description: Capcom disclosed a data breach exposing 11.7 million email addresses and account details after hackers accessed its CAPCOM ID service. Japanese gaming company Capcom has disclosed a data breach discovered on October 19 involving its CAPCOM ID service, which provides access to online services and games. As of October 22, attackers stole 11,774,247 email addresses, along with account details including creation dates, last login dates, login counts, and the IP addresses used for the latest logins. “We have recently discovered that unauthorized access by a third party occurred to our online membership service “CAPCOM ID” (*1) , resulting in the leakage of some customer information.” reads the company’s notice . “Number of leaked email addresses and system-specific identification information: 11,774,247 (worldwide total)” In 43 cases, hackers exposed date of birth, gender, country/region, and nickname. Capcom also reported that attackers illegally changed passwords on 196 accounts, and the company has already reset them. The company said the incident exposed personal information belonging to a small number of individuals. Capcom has activated its incident response procedures and confirmed that services using CAPCOM ID remain operational. The company has notified the relevant authorities, is investigating the breach, and has begun contacting affected customers through a dedicated support channel. The company also urges users to watch out for phishing attempts involving emails impersonating Capcom or its partners, particularly those containing suspicious links or attachments. It says it will investigate the incident, address the identified causes, and strengthen its security measures to prevent similar breaches. “In response, we implemented emergency measures and began identifying and addressing the attack method.” states the notice.”A task force was established within the company to gather information and take measures to prevent further damage. The investigation revealed that some customer information registered with “CAPCOM ID” had been leaked. In addition, unauthorized password changes were confirmed for some accounts. On the same day, the incident was reported to the Security Oversight Committee, our external advisory organization.” Capcom was previously targeted by the Ragnar Locker ransomware gang in November 2020 . The attackers claimed to have stolen 1 TB of data, potentially affecting up to 390,000 people. item.title: [Data Breach] ENGIE Data Breach Exposes Customer Details and Energy Contracts
item.description: ENGIE says attackers accessed French customers’ contact and energy contract data through a partner sales tool. Banking data was not affected. French multinational energy company ENGIE warned customers in France that attackers accessed personal information through a sales tool used by some business partners. The exposed data includes contact details and energy contract information that could help fraudsters impersonate the supplier. The company says its internal IT systems weren’t compromised and banking information wasn’t affected. It has blocked the attackers’ access, notified the relevant authorities and contacted affected customers, according to a spokesperson who spoke to BleepingComputer . According to notification emails sent to affected customers, the incident involved a tool used by partners to sell the company’s electricity and natural gas offers. The notification confirms that attackers gained unauthorized access to personal information stored in the sales tool. “We are informing you that an act of cyber-malice recently affected a tool used by some of our partners to market energy offers. As part of this incident, unauthorized access to your personal data was identified.” reads the notification . The compromised information includes customers’ names, postal addresses, email addresses, telephone numbers, customer IDs, contract numbers and energy supply identifiers. The company hasn’t disclosed the partner or platform involved. It also hasn’t revealed how many customers were affected, when the intrusion began, or when it was discovered. For electricity customers, these include the delivery point identifier (PDL). For gas customers, they include the metering and estimation point (PCE). ENGIE says financial information wasn’t affected and that its investigation indicates the exposure was limited to contact details and certain contract information. That reduces one category of risk but doesn’t eliminate financial fraud. Attackers can use accurate customer information to persuade victims to disclose additional data or make payments. Anyway, the exposed data could support impersonation scams. The company warned customers to watch for attempts to obtain further information or induce payments. A contract number, however, doesn’t prove that a caller is legitimate. It may simply show that the person has access to an exposed record. Customers should verify unexpected requests through trusted channels, even when the sender knows their personal details. ENGIE hasn’t attributed the attack to a specific group, and at this time no ransomware group has claimed responsibility for the attack. Experts recommend visiting ENGIE’s official website or app directly instead of signing in through links received by email. Customers should also be cautious with unexpected calls and messages. If someone requests a payment, password or additional personal information, they should end the exchange and verify the request using independently obtained official contact details. Customers should never share SMS verification codes, passwords or banking details with someone who contacts them unexpectedly. item.title: [Data Breach] Hacker leaks data on more than 40,000 Homeland Security employees
item.description: A hacker leaks personal data on more than 40,000 DHS employees, including CBP, ICE and CISA staff, after an undisclosed breach. Personal details of thousands of U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) employees are now online after a hacker stole reams of data in a data breach that occurred earlier this year and nobody had disclosed. “The breach includes names, job titles, and work contact information, such as email addresses, cell phone numbers, and office locations, of more than 40,000 people who work for the federal department, including border and immigration agents, cybersecurity staffers, and senior department officials.” TechCrunch reports . The incident impacted border and immigration agents, cybersecurity staff and senior department officials. DHS confirmed it is aware of a potential breach and is investigating, saying it takes threats to employees seriously and will provide updates when more information is available. “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively. We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available,” a DHS spokesperson told SecurityWeek. The hacker, who uses the name Department of Peace, claims to have stolen the data from an Okta single sign-on system. DHS uses this service to give employees and contractors across its agencies access to the department’s central network. The system also stores IT and login records for each account, showing which systems and internal apps each person can access. The hacker left a note with the leaked data, seen by TechCrunch, saying that if others have their information, it is only fair to share theirs. The malicious actor did not reveal how the U.S. agency was breached. More than half of the records, around 21,000, belong to U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) employees working at airports and other ports of entry. Another 10,000 belong to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and its Homeland Security Investigations unit, while just under 1,000 are linked to the cybersecurity agency CISA. Thousands of other records belong to DHS headquarters and agencies such as U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and the Federal Protective Service. DDoSecrets says the leaked database identifies officials involved in undercover operations and key DHS personnel overseeing renditions and deportations. Department of Peace said the leak was a response to the government’s actions against ICE. Crimew described the database as an unprecedented view of DHS’s organizational structure, helping researchers identify employees, their roles and reporting lines. They said it could also support investigations and future Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests. DDoSecrets co-founder Emma Best said the database, called Icepick , identifies officials involved in covert operations, internal investigations and deportation programs. Ryan Shapiro of Property of the People added that employee contact details could help researchers submit more targeted FOIA requests. Best said the data could also support journalism, congressional inquiries, legal challenges and community investigations. “Rather than an indiscriminate directory of every DHS employee, Icepick identifies many of the architects and drivers of DHS policy and operations,” said journalist and DDoSecrets cofounder Emma Best. “The leak is extraordinary but deceptive in its simplicity as it identifies the officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations, the government’s hunt for leakers and the failed BlueLeaks investigation — along with key personnel in DHS’s ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs.” “By replacing the regime’s anonymity with accountability, Icepick and the tool developed by maia are catalyst for investigations, empowering journalists, Congressional inquiries, legal challenges, community action and Freedom of Information Act requests,” added Best. DHS is investigating a potential breach. Okta says it has no evidence its systems or data were compromised. The breach follows other attacks on U.S. government agencies that exposed FBI records and military personnel data . It is also the second DHS breach this year, after the same hacker claimed to have stolen thousands of government contracts. Journalist maia arson crimew shared the data with DDoSecrets. TechCrunch verified some records, which suggest the database was copied around mid-August. The leak covers about one-fifth of DHS’s 220,000 employees. The records reveal access to tools including Microsoft 365, ChatGPT, Penlink surveillance software and Mobile Fortify, a facial recognition app used by CBP and ICE. Around 4,500 accounts belong to a Headspace user group, while more than 2,000 Homeland Security Investigations employees appear in Penlink-related groups. Researchers say the contact details could help journalists file targeted Freedom of Information Act requests. However, exposing employees’ phone numbers and office locations also creates security and privacy risks. item.title: [HaveIBeenPwned] AfD - 345,439 breached accounts
item.description: In September 2026, the German political party Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) suffered a data breach which exposed 345k unique email addresses. The following month, hundreds of gigabytes of data containing hundreds of thousands of emails and attachments was published online, with searchable AI-generated summaries and downloadable original files. An analysis of the incident reported that the breach was detected as early as 9 September, with a subsequent intrusion occurring five days later. In its public statement , AfD attributed the breach to an attack on a hosting provider, identified in subsequent reporting as the party-owned Alternita Dienstleistungs GmbH.
